text: Can you solve all seven? This is the seven out of seven challenge.
Seven riddles to test your logic. Sixty seconds for each one.
Grab a pen, write down your answers, and comment your score at the end. Let's see who gets seven out of seven.
Riddle number one, to warm up.
A bat and a ball cost one dollar and ten cents in total.
The bat costs one dollar more than the ball.
How much does the ball cost?
Sixty seconds. Write your answer, or vote in the comments. Go!
Time's up! Did you say ten cents? That's the answer most people give first.
But then the bat would cost one dollar and ten cents, and together they'd cost one dollar and twenty cents.
The real answer is five cents: five cents plus one dollar and five cents makes exactly one dollar and ten cents.
If you got it, give yourself a point.
Riddle two is a little harder.
A patch of lily pads doubles in size every day.
On day forty-eight, it covers the whole lake.
On which day did it cover half the lake?
Sixty seconds. Comment your answer before time runs out. Go!
Time's up! It's day forty-seven.
If the patch doubles every day, one day before the lake is full, it was half full.
Many people say day twenty-four, because our brains think in straight lines, not in doublings.
Got it? That's another point.
Riddle three is where it gets tricky.
You have two ropes and a lighter.
Each rope takes exactly one hour to burn, but unevenly: half a rope doesn't always take half an hour.
How can you measure exactly forty-five minutes?
Sixty seconds. Think it through, then type your method in the comments. Go!
Time's up! Light the first rope at both ends and the second rope at one end, at the same time.
The first rope burns out in exactly thirty minutes.
At that moment, light the other end of the second rope: its last thirty minutes now burn in fifteen.
Thirty plus fifteen: forty-five minutes.
If you found this one, your logic is sharp.
Riddle four.
In one of our Shorts, we showed that a pair of pants has two holes.
So how many holes does a T-shirt have?
One: four. Two: three. Three: zero.
Sixty seconds. Vote now: comment one, two, or three. Go!
Time's up! The answer is three.
A T-shirt has four openings: the neck, the bottom, and two sleeves.
For a single piece like this, holes equal openings minus one.
Four minus one: three holes.
Riddle five.
A rope is wrapped tightly around the Earth's equator, about twenty-five thousand miles long.
You add just three feet of rope and lift it evenly all around the planet.
How high does it float?
One: the width of a hair. Two: about six inches. Three: about a mile.
Sixty seconds. Vote: one, two, or three. Go!
Time's up! About six inches.
A circle's length is two pi times its radius, so three more feet lifts the rope by three feet divided by two pi: about five point seven inches, all the way around.
A mouse could walk under it.
And the strange part: you'd get the same gap around a basketball.
Riddle six.
How many people do you need in a room for a better than fifty-fifty chance that two of them share a birthday?
One: twenty-three. Two: one hundred eighty-three. Three: three hundred sixty-six.
Sixty seconds. Lock in your vote in the comments. Go!
Time's up! Just twenty-three.
We imagine someone sharing our own birthday, but twenty-three people make two hundred fifty-three different pairs, and every pair is a chance for a match.
At twenty-three people, the odds pass fifty percent.
With seventy, they're over ninety-nine percent.
And riddle seven, the final boss.
This one fooled even mathematicians.
On a game show, there are three doors: a car behind one, goats behind the other two.
You pick door one. The host, who knows where the car is, opens door three: a goat.
Should you stay, or switch to door two?
One: stay. Two: switch. Three: it doesn't matter.
Last sixty seconds. Final vote: one, two, or three. Go!
Time's up! Switch. Switching wins two times out of three.
Your first pick had a one in three chance; the other two doors together had two in three.
The host always opens a goat door, so he just shows you which of those two to take.
When this puzzle ran in a magazine in nineteen ninety, thousands of readers, some with PhDs, wrote in to say the answer was wrong.
It wasn't.
Time to count your points.
Zero to two: your brain is warming up. Three or four: solid logic. Five or six: you've got a sharp mind. Seven out of seven: genius level.
Now comment your score, and tell us which riddle got you!
And subscribe to Factora, so you never miss a new challenge.
